title: The Secrets of the Great Pyramid

pages.text: Mr Bonsu placed a model pyramid on his desk. “The Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt was built more than 4,000 years ago. It was about 147 metres tall, as high as a 45-storey building. It contains about 2.3 million blocks, each weighing between 2.5 and 15 tonnes.” Fatawu whistled. “Why is it a mystery?”
sentences: Mr Bonsu placed a model pyramid on his desk.
“The Great Pyramid of Giza in Egypt was built more than 4,000 years ago.
It was about 147 metres tall, as high as a 45-storey building.
It contains about 2.3 million blocks, each weighing between 2.5 and 15 tonnes.” Fatawu whistled.
“Why is it a mystery?”
pages.alt: A teacher places a model pyramid on his desk in front of the class.

pages.text: Naana worked it out. “If they built it in about twenty years, that is more than 100,000 blocks a year, and about 300 every day.” “That is about 12 or 13 blocks every hour, day and night,” said Fatawu. “It must have been very organised.” “Exactly,” said Mr Bonsu. “So who organised it, and how?”

“It must have been very organised.” “Exactly,” said Mr Bonsu.
“So who organised it, and how?”
pages.alt: Students do sums on the board about blocks per year, day and hour.

pages.text: “A discovery gave us a clue,” said Mr Bonsu. “Between 2011 and 2013, a team led by archaeologist Pierre Tallet found papyrus logbooks at a place called Wadi al-Jarf, near the Red Sea. A crew leader named Merer wrote about hauling limestone blocks to the pyramid.” “A diary from 4,500 years ago!” said Naana.

A crew leader named Merer wrote about hauling limestone blocks to the pyramid.” “A diary from 4,500 years ago!” said Naana.
pages.alt: Archaeologists unroll an ancient papyrus logbook in a desert cave.

pages.text: “Merer’s crew carried the stone on boats,” said Mr Bonsu. “And in 2024, scientists using satellite radar found an old branch of the Nile, about 64 kilometres long, running beside around thirty pyramids. It may have helped workers float stone and supplies close to the building sites.” “So the river was a highway,” said Fatawu.

pages.alt: A map shows an ancient branch of the river beside several pyramids, with boats carrying stone.

pages.text: “But how did they lift the blocks up the pyramid?” asked Naana. “That,” said Mr Bonsu, “is still debated. Ramps, levers, ropes and sledges are part of the likely answer. The exact method, and how steep the ramps were, are not settled.” Fatawu sketched four ideas.

pages.text: “And here is a new puzzle,” said Mr Bonsu. “Scientists have found a large cavity above a long passage inside the pyramid called the Grand Gallery. We do not yet know what it is for, or what is in it.” Naana’s eyes widened. “A secret room?” “We do not know,” said Mr Bonsu.

We do not yet know what it is for, or what is in it.” Naana’s eyes widened.
“A secret room?” “We do not know,” said Mr Bonsu.
pages.alt: A cutaway drawing of a pyramid with a hollow space above a long gallery.

pages.text: Fatawu tapped the logbook picture. “So it was not magic and not aliens,” he said. “It was people: organised, skilled and working together.” “Why does that matter?” asked Mr Bonsu. “Because it gives credit to the workers,” said Naana. “Real people did this. They had plans, boats, ropes and teams.”

pages.text: At the end, the class wrote: Solved (mostly): who built it and that boats and a river helped. Debated: how the blocks were lifted. Unknown: what the hidden space is. “The most amazing mystery,” said Fatawu, “is that people long ago did something we still admire.” Mr Bonsu nodded. The end.

A paper-like material made from a reed plant, used for writing long ago.
